brief: Where creative direction comes from when nobody hands you a brief

slots.eyebrow: On having to decide it yourself
slots.titleLine1: Nobody is going to tell you
slots.subtitle: Six places direction actually comes from once there is no client, no brand guide and no art director to disagree with.
slots.item1: Why a reference is not a direction
slots.item2: The constraint that does the deciding for you
slots.coverNote: The last one is why most of this is harder than it sounds

slots.body: References tell you what you like, which is a very long list and settles nothing. One real constraint — a single colour, one typeface, no photography — eliminates most of the options before you have to have an opinion about them, and the remaining decisions are the ones worth making.
slots.p1Body: Before the ideas, so it shapes them rather than filtering them afterwards.
slots.p2Body: A constraint you would have chosen anyway is not doing any work.
slots.p3Title: Keep it for the whole piece
slots.p3Body: A rule abandoned halfway leaves the work looking undecided rather than free.

slots.body: Surface copies age immediately and read as derivative to anyone who saw the original. What survives borrowing is the underlying decision — the proportion, the rhythm, the way the thing withholds information — and almost nobody can see you took it.
slots.p1Body: If you cannot say what it does, you are copying the finish.
slots.p2Body: What you remember is the structure. What you forget was decoration.
slots.p3Body: The same structure in a different medium stops being a reference.

slots.body: Not a mood, an adjective you would defend: austere, generous, abrupt, warm. It is the only test that resolves an argument between two options that both look fine, and without it you will pick whichever you made most recently.
slots.p1Body: Two words is a compromise and will produce a compromise.
slots.p2Body: Ask which option is more austere, not which one you prefer.
slots.p3Body: If it embarrasses you slightly, it is specific enough to be useful.

slots.body: At small size only arrangement survives, and arrangement is the part that decides whether anything works. Starting large lets you fix a broken structure with detail, which produces work that is immaculate up close and confused from across the room.
slots.p1Body: Six arrangements at postcard size beats one at full size.
slots.p2Body: Craft applied early defends decisions that should have been changed.
slots.p3Body: Anything that only works at one of them is not finished.

slots.body: A polished first attempt is impossible to judge, because the finish flatters the decision underneath it. Building the deliberately crude version takes an hour and reveals whether there is anything there other than execution.
slots.p1Body: Default settings, wrong typeface, no spacing decisions at all.
slots.p2Body: This one is for you. Feedback on a rough version is about the roughness.
slots.p3Body: Whatever survives being made badly is the actual idea.

slots.body: None of this reveals a right answer, because there is not one waiting to be found. Every method here exists to get you to commit sooner, and the work that reads as having a strong direction is usually just work where somebody stopped considering alternatives early.
slots.p1Body: Certainty arrives from the work, never before it.
slots.p2Body: One decision applied everywhere looks deliberate. Six good ones do not.
slots.p3Body: That is true of every piece you admire, including the ones that look inevitable.

slots.eyebrow: On the thing you keep restarting
slots.body: One colour, or one typeface, or one thing you will not do. Apply it to the whole piece without exception and see what it decides on your behalf.
slots.closingLine: The direction was never out there. It is whichever constraint you were willing to keep.
slots.signoff: Commitment is what reads as taste
